text: A state gets made by compromise, and the man who signs for it inherits the anger of everyone who wanted more. Neil Jordan shoots 1920s Ireland as a thriller before he shoots it as history: informers, safe houses, a war conducted in doorways and on bicycles. The prizes it took point at how it works — a Golden Lion, a Volpi Cup for the lead performance, Academy awards for cinematography and for the dramatic score. Image and music carry the dread the dialogue keeps courteous. Then the fight turns inward, and a good share of the 132 minutes goes to rooms where men decide what a country will settle for. That is the part the film treats as dangerous. It was made in Ireland about the founding of the Irish Free State, which is to say it is arguing with its own audience.

Wednesday afternoons, one address, no names exchanged — an arrangement that works precisely because neither party has to account for the rest of the week. Patrice Chéreau films the sex first and the biography second, which reverses the usual order and makes the biography, when it comes, feel like an intrusion rather than a reward. The setting is London and the language is English; the production is French, and the film keeps a stranger's eye on a city it treats as a place where a person can stay unknown at will. It carries a Golden Bear, a Silver Bear for its lead performance, and the European Film Awards' best film. What the arrangement withholds is context, and the moment a man decides he wants some — following her, learning what she does with her other days — the terms that protected him stop working.

A car overheats in the desert, a man stops for water, and a mother superior decides God has sent her a builder. The joke is that neither side can leave: he has no money and she has no bricklayer, and the negotiation between an unemployed construction worker and a house of East European nuns is carried out in an English that neither side fully owns. Ninety-four minutes, black and white, 1963 — a small American picture running on labour and stubbornness rather than plot. The record around it is not small: an Academy award for the lead performance, a Silver Bear for the same, cinematography and best picture citations, the National Board of Review's ten, and later the National Film Registry. What holds it together is the question of who is doing whom the favour, which nobody will concede.

Competitive ballroom is a sport with a rulebook, and in this film the rulebook is the villain. Scott dances steps of his own invention; the federation treats that as a disciplinary matter rather than a question of taste, and the comedy runs on exactly that confusion between authority and judgement. Baz Luhrmann keeps it to ninety-four minutes and stages the suburban Australian dance circuit at the scale of an operetta — costume, lighting and grievance all pitched several sizes above life. The Australian academy gave it best film and its lead and supporting acting awards, and audiences handed it a people's choice prize, a pairing that does not happen often. What survives the glitter is the partnership, and the fact that the risk belongs to whoever has least to lose by breaking a rule.

A brother comes back to the town his sister never left, and neither of them has a plan for what that is supposed to repair. Kenneth Lonergan writes the argument families actually have — circular, affectionate, unwinnable — and gives it no crisis to hang on. There is a single mother with a job and a son. There is a younger man who arrives with less than he implies. The rest is a hundred and eleven minutes of two adults negotiating a shared childhood from opposite conclusions about it. The Academy cited the screenplay and the lead performance, the Writers Guild the screenplay again, and a Grand Jury Prize came with them; for a film this undramatic, that amounts to a verdict on the writing. Lonergan's interest is in the sentences people almost say.

The occupation it stages ran through 1944; the film carries the date 1945. A hunted man in an occupied city needs doors that will open for him, which turns neighbours, stairwells and landlords into the machinery of the plot — Roberto Rossellini builds Roma città aperta out of that dependence rather than out of combat. A hundred and four minutes, made in Italy within a year of the events themselves, with almost no retrospect available to it. The record is long: a Palme d'Or, an Academy citation for the adapted screenplay, a place on the Cahiers du Cinéma hundred and on Italy's own register of films to be saved. Its force comes from proximity — ordinary domestic noise and lethal risk one floor apart, in the same building.

Two hundred minutes is not a length, it is a claim: that a private attachment can be followed all the way through a revolution without either being reduced to background. David Lean's physician writes poems, marries one woman and loves another while the First World War and then October rearrange the country underneath him. The Academy prizes went to colour cinematography, art direction and costume, which is honest about where the film puts its case — it argues for the private life in fabric, glass, weather and rooms. It travels further on a Golden Globe for best drama, a screenplay citation, the National Board of Review's ten, and the BFI's hundred British films. The scale is enormous and the subject is small on purpose, and Lean never lets the second be an excuse for the first.

A kid in a north Dublin estate decides that what his neighbourhood needs is American soul, and starts auditioning. Nothing in The Commitments treats that as a metaphor. Jimmy Rabbitte wants a band, wants it tight, and the film gives its attention to logistics: an advertisement, a trumpet player twice everyone's age, three voices found within walking distance, a singer discovered at a wedding. Alan Parker cuts fast enough that rehearsal carries the story, and the Academy's editing award — along with a place on the BFI's hundred British films — sits with the craft rather than the sentiment. A hundred and eighteen minutes in which the funniest material and the most serious material are the same material: people with no leverage deciding to be professional about something.

Seventy-five minutes is barely a feature, and this one gives them to a single bad decision and the hours immediately after it. Three young women break into a mansion they take to be empty. The break-in is the easy part. What follows is closer to a chamber piece than a chase: few rooms, few people, and a disagreement that grows teeth as the night goes on. Robert Olsen keeps the machinery in plain sight, so the pressure comes from consensus rather than pursuit — competing accounts of the same minute, and no arrangement in which everyone can be right. The genres attached to it run from drama to horror, and it moves between them without changing rooms. It works on the oldest terms in the form: friends who trusted each other at midnight, and something to lose an hour later.

Three people, three positions in one war: an émigré Russian noblewoman working with the French resistance, a French official who collaborates, and an SS officer with rank. Andrei Konchalovsky sets them against each other and refuses the arrangement in which one of the three is simply the audience's seat. That is the hard part — the film lets a man who believes in the Reich speak at length and in his own terms, which puts the work of sorting explanation from justification back where it belongs. A hundred and thirty minutes, in Russian, about Europe. It carries a Silver Lion for direction, Russia's Golden Eagle and Nika for best picture, and a national submission to the Academy Awards. Its subject is not the war but the accounting people do while they are still inside it.

Monday is the word that does the damage: for men with work it starts something, and for these men it is another afternoon at Rico's bar. The shipyard in northern Spain has closed, and Santa, José and the rest have kept the shape of the week without its content — a court case over a lamp smashed at a protest, a wife employed while her husband is not, hours to be filled in daylight. Fernando León de Aranoa lets the comedy come from the talk, which is constant, and the drama from what the talk holds at bay. A hundred and thirteen minutes, a Goya for best film, a Golden Shell, a European prize for its lead actor, and Spain's submission to the Academy Awards. It is unusually attentive to the fact that unemployment is mostly a problem of time.

A newsroom is where the ethical question and the romantic one arrive in the same person, at speed. James L. Brooks gives his producer a mind that cuts a segment faster than anyone can talk her out of it, then sets in front of her a reporter with the substance and an anchor with the face, and declines to make the choice a matter of the heart alone. The Academy cited both leads and the cinematography, a Silver Bear went to a lead performance, the New York critics named it the year's best film, and it later entered the National Film Registry. What earns that is the procedure — feeds, countdowns, a piece cut with seconds left — which the film shoots as suspense and as a moral test at once. A hundred and thirty-three minutes of people very good at a job they suspect is getting worse.

An actor is handed the role of his life at exactly the wrong moment in his country's history, and cannot bring himself to refuse it. István Szabó keeps the camera inside the theatre while the politics do their work offstage: colleagues leaving the country, new patrons arriving in the better seats, a repertoire quietly adjusting itself. A hundred and forty-five minutes in German, made in 1981 about the years the Nazis took power, and specific in a way period films rarely are about how a career is actually built — largely by not saying the sentence that would end it. It carries the Academy's award for an international feature, a screenplay prize, and a place on the German list of the films that matter most. The subject is a man performing, and the performance goes all the way down.

Most of this film is ordinary traffic between people: family, friends, a favour owed, strangers met once and not again. Ryan Coogler's first feature covers a single day in Oakland and declines nearly every device available to it — no investigation, no thesis spoken aloud, nobody explaining what the day amounts to. What it does instead is accumulate. Oscar Grant is written inconsistent: generous, evasive, unfinished, harder to write than a saint and harder to set aside. Eighty-two minutes, short enough that nothing in it reads as filler. It took the Sundance audience award and a Grand Jury Prize, the New York critics' first-film prize, a place on the National Board of Review's ten, and the Stanley Kramer Award. Its argument is carried by proportion alone.
